Gold Sniping:Finding Gold Where It Hides Underwater

An illustrated field guide to underwater gold traps, techniques, equipment, and the science of where gold settles.

By Paul Shoemaker · Gold Trails
Research edition · Reviewed November 2, 2026 · 5 sections

Gold sniping is the close-up search for gold in submerged cracks, pockets and other small traps. A clear view can reveal details a pan cannot: the shape of a crevice, the layers of its fill, and sometimes a particle before it moves. The real skill is learning what those details do—and do not—tell you.

Look closely. Sample carefully.A promising feature is a place to ask a question.
Gold is never guaranteed.

!

Before you get in: cold water, current and slippery bedrock can be dangerous even in shallow water. Keep clear of submerged gaps and unstable rocks. Confirm permission and permitted methods. Read Safety & Access →

Field guide / 01

Read the river.
Then test your hunch.

A crack is a clue. A sample is evidence. Explore six places where gold might be retained—and the reasons each can come up empty.

01Bedrock crevices02Boulder bases03Natural potholes04Bedrock ledges & steps05Clay & false-bedrock contacts06Submerged gravel pockets

Bedrock crevices

A narrow opening can shelter dense particles when the surrounding bed is disturbed. A crack is a possible retaining structure, not evidence of gold.

Where to compare
Test retained sediment at the bottom, beneath small lodged stones, and along changes in the crack’s width. Visible surface flakes do not establish what lies below.
What flow changes
An open crack may admit sediment during stronger flow and retain some as flow declines. Orientation, packing, and later floods change the outcome.
Why it can disappoint
The crack may be sealed, recently emptied, outside the gold-bearing transport path, or filled with barren recent sediment.
Try a small testIf permitted and safely reachable from a stable position, photograph the undisturbed fill. Sample the top and deeper fill separately, without prying apart bedrock; compare equal volumes with nearby loose sediment.

Boulder bases

A stable boulder changes local flow. Its base and protected pockets may retain heavy particles while nearby accelerated flow removes sediment.

Where to compare
Compare accessible downstream pockets, side contacts, and sediment immediately against the base. Do not assume the downstream side always wins.
What flow changes
Flow accelerates around an obstacle and can scour its sides or base; a changing wake can either deposit or remove sediment. Flood flow may differ from today’s gentle current.
Why it can disappoint
The boulder may have moved, its wake may be actively scouring, or the retained gravel may contain no gold supply.
Try a small testCompare equal-volume samples from safely accessible side and downstream pockets. Never reach beneath an unstable boulder, shift it, or enter a constricted current.

Natural potholes

A depression provides space for sediment to accumulate, but the same circulating water that forms a pothole may keep its contents moving.

Where to compare
Where access is safe and legal, compare loose upper fill with retained material near the bottom or under an existing rim. Gold can be absent at every level.
What flow changes
Circulating flow can grind and scour a pothole during floods. Material preserved after falling flow need not represent a permanent trap.
Why it can disappoint
An apparently deep pocket may have been flushed clean, filled only recently, or isolated from gold-bearing sediment.
Try a small testObserve from above. Sample only a small, shallow depression reachable without submerging your head or putting a hand into a blind opening. Keep layers separate; leave deep or obstructed holes alone.

Bedrock ledges & steps

A step interrupts the bed surface and may create a protected contact or a sediment pocket. Whether it retains gold depends on the local flow and sediment supply.

Where to compare
Compare the foot of the step, any accessible seam, and sediment farther downstream. A bare ledge is a feature to investigate, not a pay streak.
What flow changes
A jet over the step can scour the landing area while quieter adjacent pockets retain material. Later floods may reverse what appears promising at low water.
Why it can disappoint
The step may focus erosive flow directly into the pocket, or the pocket may receive only recently deposited barren sand.
Try a small testFrom a stable shallow position, compare small samples at the foot and beside the step. Avoid waterfalls, undercuts, hydraulic recirculation, and slippery drop-offs.

Clay & false-bedrock contacts

A resistant layer can interrupt downward movement and provide a contact at which sediment is retained. Clay alone neither attracts gold nor proves a deposit.

Where to compare
Compare material immediately above the firm contact with overlying loose gravel. If allowed, keep any naturally exposed seam material separate.
What flow changes
A firm surface may persist while looser material is reworked; erosion can also cut through or strip it. Today’s surface may not be the concentrating surface of an earlier flood.
Why it can disappoint
The clay may be recent or discontinuous, the contact may be barren, or fine gold may occur in a different layer. Firm material is not necessarily true bedrock.
Try a small testRecord texture and layer order. Compare equal volumes above the contact and higher in the gravel without cutting banks, excavating clay, or assuming the hard layer marks the end of the gold.

Submerged gravel pockets

A hollow in bedrock can retain a patch of gravel after nearby material moves. Such pockets preserve a local sediment history rather than guaranteeing a concentrate.

Where to compare
Compare the exposed surface, material beneath existing small stones, and sediment at the bedrock contact. Do not mix these before recording them.
What flow changes
Floods may load, sort, or flush the pocket. Coarse grains can armor finer sediment, while strong flow may remove the entire fill.
Why it can disappoint
The gravel may be too recently deposited, derived from a barren source, or repeatedly flushed without retaining gold.
Try a small testPhotograph the pocket, label small surface and contact samples, and compare equivalent volumes with a neighboring pocket. Log empty samples alongside positive results.
Explore the diagram

These are Gold Trails’ conceptual sampling suggestions. USGS describes fractured bedrock, natural riffles and gravel above clay as placer settings; the Forest Service/BLM field guide also identifies candidate traps. Neither source proves gold is present in a particular feature. For the broader picture, read Where Gold Settles in a River.

Field guide / 02

Slow hands. Clear water.
Better observations.

Start with what you can see from above. This is a shallow-water observation and sampling guide; it does not teach breath-hold or scuba diving.

  1. Look before you touch

    From a stable, shallow position, use a viewer to study the undisturbed bottom. Photograph the feature and record the apparent gold position before stirring sediment. A yellow flash remains an identification question; keep uncertain material separate.

  2. Make the water your window

    A viewing bucket rests its clear base in the surface to reduce glare and ripples. Stay where you can keep your footing and head above water. Stop when turbidity or reflections prevent you seeing your hands and the bed clearly.

  3. Sample a small, accessible patch

    Confirm that your tools and method are allowed. Use a small hand crevice tool only in visible, reachable sediment; do not pry apart bedrock, move boulders or put a hand into an unseen opening. Let suspended sediment clear before continuing.

  4. Keep the layers separate

    Collect surface fill, deeper retained fill and contact material in separate labeled containers. Mixing layers loses the information you are trying to learn. Where a layer is inaccessible or would require damaging excavation, leave it untested and record that limit.

  5. Recover, then check the rejects

    Transfer tiny visible particles to a labeled container or a hand collection device only where that device is permitted. Pan sediment and retain the tailings for a second check. Recovery losses can make a productive sample look empty.

  6. Write down the misses, too

    Record trap, layer, sample volume, water conditions, method and result—including zero gold. Compare similar volumes with the same recovery method. A result from one pocket does not rank an entire river.

Field guide / 03

Start with a clear view.
Keep the kit simple.

Buy for the task you can safely and legally do. A viewer, a few hand tools and good sample records are more useful than a pile of expensive equipment.

01Essential for viewing

A window into the stream

A viewing bucket or underwater viewer is the simplest starting point for observation from above. Choose a clear, secure base and a size you can use without leaning beyond stable footing. An expensive camera is optional.

02Essential for sampling

Small hand tools

A blunt crevice probe, small scoop and pan are enough for accessible, permitted sediment samples. Choose tools you can control in plain sight. Motorized equipment and suction tools are not a default part of this kit.

03Essential for records

Containers & labels

Bring separate leak-resistant containers, a secure sample vial, waterproof labels and a pencil. Keep layers and locations separate. A simple notebook helps you learn more than a single bottle of mixed material.

04Essential for protection

Grip, warmth & flotation

Use footwear with suitable wet-rock traction, hand protection appropriate to the task and clothing chosen for the water temperature. Use a properly fitted flotation device appropriate to the activity. None of this equipment makes hazardous current safe.

05Optional · training dependent

Mask & snorkel

A properly fitting mask can improve underwater visibility. A snorkel is breathing equipment, not protection from current or cold. It is not required for a viewer-based outing; seek appropriate instruction before face-in-water activity.

06Optional

A little light

A small waterproof light may help in an accessible shadow. Secure loose items without creating snag or entrapment hazards. Poor visibility, depth or a blind crevice is a reason to stop, not a reason to buy a brighter light.

Equipment categories are editorial suggestions, not product endorsements. Check permitted collection devices before buying. NWS cold-water guidance explains why water temperature and flotation matter. Read Safety & Access before entering the water.

Field guide / 04

Good clues deserve
honest evidence.

Gold is dense. Rivers are complicated. Separate a demonstrated position, a creator’s explanation and a geological model before drawing a conclusion.

Observed in the field

Requires an identifiable source moment and a record of what is actually visible. No independently reviewed underwater recovery is claimed here.

Creator interpretation

A useful explanation to investigate. Video titles and chapter labels alone do not verify where gold sat or how it arrived.

Scientific background

Published descriptions support general processes. They do not establish a productive pocket at your site.

USGS explains that gold’s high density helps it concentrate as high water agitates stream sediment. The USGS placer model describes fractured bedrock, basal gravel and gravel over clay among favorable settings. Density is one part of the story: sediment supply, particle size and shape, flood history and the survival of a pocket all matter.

A low-water eddy does not tell you exactly what happened during a flood. A downstream boulder pocket may preserve gravel while an adjacent jet scours the bed; a pothole can collect material and later empty. Our diagrams offer comparison positions, not universal winning sides. Read Seven Prospecting Rules Worth Questioning for related caption-derived accounts and their stated limits.

Scientific & field references

  1. Gold — Harold Kirkemo, William L. Newman and Roger P. Ashley · U.S. Geological Survey. Explains gold's high density and concentration on or near bedrock as moving stream sediment is agitated during high water. General process guidance, not a prediction for an individual crevice.
  2. Descriptive model of Placer Au–PGE · Model 39a — Warren E. Yeend · USGS Bulletin 1693 (1986). Describes gold concentrations associated with fractured bedrock, natural riffles, basal gravel and gravel above clay layers. The model describes deposit settings; it does not verify any diagrammed trap.
  3. Gold Panning · 2018 revision · printed page 8 — U.S. Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management. Identifies bedrock crevices, pockets, downstream sides of boulders and impermeable clay contacts as candidate sampling settings. This is a Kenai Peninsula guide; its access rules and seasonal advice are not transferred to New England.
Field guide / 05

The best find is
getting home safely.

Choose the conditions before choosing the trap. A promising crack never justifies cold exposure, unstable footing, hazardous flow or uncertain permission.

Cold is an immediate hazard

Cold shock can interfere with breathing before hypothermia develops. Dress for the water, plan a short exposure with a dry change of clothing and use appropriate flotation. Stop at the first loss of comfort or control. Read NWS cold-water guidance.

Currents change the rules

Avoid rapids, constrictions, waterfalls and hydraulic recirculation. Calm-looking water can hide strong current. Check upstream rain, forecasts, gauges and dam-release notices; leave well before water rises. NPS river-safety guidance describes these hazards.

Never reach into a blind trap

Do not work under unstable boulders, undercuts or submerged logs. Keep hands and feet out of narrow gaps and avoid trailing straps or loose gear. If you cannot see the bottom and a clear route out, do not enter.

Plan the way out first

Wet bedrock can be extremely slippery. Choose a stable position and a clear exit. Work with a companion who knows the plan; leave if visibility deteriorates. This article does not qualify anyone to dive, hold their breath underwater or enter hazardous current.

Maine & New England: check the method and the place

Permission to stand beside a river is not permission to remove its sediment. Confirm ownership, land-manager rules, protected habitat, claims where applicable, permitted tools and seasonal restrictions. Cold water can remain hazardous even on a warm day.

Maine

Maine’s gold-panning exemption has conditions, including limits on bank disturbance and discharges; motorized prospecting has separate rules. A panning exemption does not automatically authorize crevicing or every suction device. In unorganized and deorganized areas under its jurisdiction, consult LUPC’s recreational-prospecting guidance and confirm your exact site and method with the agency. Obtain landowner permission.

Across state lines

New England does not have one prospecting rulebook. For example, Vermont DEC distinguishes hand panning, permitted sluices and prohibited suction dredges, and calls for written permission on private land. Check the responsible state agency and land manager for each trip rather than carrying Maine assumptions into another state.

Leave the river intact

Keep disturbance small and within the rules. Protect stream banks, roots, spawning beds and aquatic habitat; do not pry apart bedrock or move large rocks. Restore disturbed sediment where required and avoid creating a sediment plume. If a sample requires damage or unsafe access, leave it in place.
